learningObjective: Order the tiers of a modern GPU memory hierarchy by latency, bandwidth and capacity, and identify design consequences.

canonicalClaims.claim: In modern NVIDIA GPUs (Ampere/Hopper), the memory tiers ordered by increasing latency and capacity but decreasing (per-SM) bandwidth are: registers < shared memory / L1 < L2 < HBM.
conditions: Ampere or newer NVIDIA architecture with standard R/S/L2/HBM hierarchy.
Aggregate bandwidth summed across SMs where relevant.
nonImplications: Does not imply L2 is only a latency shield; L2 also provides bandwidth uplift for reused data.
Does not imply that using shared memory always beats direct HBM access; small kernels may perform fine without SMEM staging.

misconceptions.claim: L2 is only a latency shield and does not add bandwidth over HBM.
misconceptions.whyWrong: L2 aggregate bandwidth exceeds HBM's; for L2-resident, reused data, L2 delivers a bandwidth multiplier in addition to latency reduction.

misconceptions.claim: HBM has the highest bandwidth of any tier in the memory hierarchy.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Off-chip HBM has high absolute bandwidth but on-chip tiers (shared memory, register file) aggregate much higher bandwidth across the whole GPU.

misconceptions.claim: Shared memory and L1 are separate structures on Ampere; you cannot trade capacity between them.
misconceptions.whyWrong: On Ampere/Hopper, shared memory and L1 share a configurable partition; software can request different splits within limits.

implementationFacts: A100: L1/SMEM up to 192 KB per SM (configurable); L2 = 40 MB; HBM ≈ 40–80 GB @ 2.0 TB/s.
H100: L2 = 50 MB; HBM3 up to ~3.35 TB/s.
performanceScenarios: GEMM tiles are sized to fit into shared memory to enable maximal reuse before writing back through L2 to HBM.
